draws.answer: Watering it once is enough, and that is what makes it last. The catalogue's instruction is to water each layer as you lay it: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a 5 cm base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 cm of manure, then about 30 cm of crop residues left or buried, with the last layer being wood ash on the topsoil. So you have all of them on a heap. Then the three things that stop it from turning: a little wood ash on the topsoil, which is the one the catalogue says to do so as a first layer, and the manure layer, which is what you watered. A layer of plant residues that has been trodden down well, or that has been burnt, is the last layer, and the word in the catalogue is "buried, rather than left on the surface", so it is not the residue that is forgotten.

Then two of its four criteria are gone. The heap is not a heap: it is a heap of residues, and the catalogue describes the build as a heap of residues that you build up in a compacted base, then lay the residues alternating layer by layer, with a little wood ash on top and a watered topsoil or well rotted compost under it. Its order is not what the catalogue asks for, which is a layer of base, then a layer of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, then a layer of manure, then a layer of plant residues trodden down well, then a layer of topsoil or well rotted compost, and so on. The watered tip at the end of it is what the catalogue does not offer as a finisher, so I have no reason to rule it out. The order matters more than anyone will notice: on a shaded site, easy to reach, shaded from the wind and the rain, and out of the way of the field, that is where the heap is meant to be, and you have to keep it there. The other five are about the same: the unit is set at 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial nucleus, the housing is improved traditional villages with a fenced run around it, the birds are given a run, they have their own droppings pit, and the plans call for a manure pit as well.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of tomato yellow leaf curl virus carried by whiteflies. First, control the whitefly by keeping the plot clean and acting early. Second, rogue out the heavily affected tomato plants that show the yellowing. Third, plant a tomato variety that is resistant to tomato yellow leaf curl virus for the next crop. You can get help with whitefly management and resistant varieties from ICAT.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer: Year one, improving plants: legumes such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean. Year two, a hungry plant that takes a lot: maize, the crop that needs the soil most. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper: yam. Year four, a fallow. After four years, the next rotation is the one the catalogue names as a rotation in its own words: cereals, then legumes.

Year one: cereals, the group the catalogue calls the best at being eaten raw or in salads. Year two: legumes, the ones named as fixing nitrogen for the soil. Year three: a root or tuber crop, the ones named as pulling out the last of the nutrients, the yam, the okra or the groundnut. Year four: a fallow. So the sequence is cereals → legumes → root crop. After four years of maize the soil is left rich in nitrogen, which is why the rotation is the one the catalogue recommends.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

Give a small dose of vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the frothy foam and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service immediately because a severe case needs their intervention without delay.

Your cattle have nagana, a trypanosomiasis spread by tsetse flies, and the disease is most common in the southern areas of Maritime and Plateaux. First, keep the animals well fed and watered so they can withstand the infection and recover. Second, reduce fly exposure by avoiding grazing in the riverine bush during the biting hours and consider fly-control measures to lower the number of flies. per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The brochure does not say, and it is a big gap, so I will not fill it. It says to keep the cereals, the legumes and the kitchen leftovers in the store past the harvest glut, and to treat them as soon as the store is ready, since a grain problem in the store is the source of much of the hunger in the country, so the store is not a safe place. But there is one other thing to take away from it that may help you. When you have finished, put the beans in an airy, dry store and sort out the mouldy ones before you start buying again. And take the rule to ICAT before you go: a store that has no grain and is not properly dried will not hold grain, and the brochure puts the store question at the front of its own advice on selling after harvest.

Selling after a harvest glut is a good time, but you still should weigh it. Look at the price you could get from neighbors, local markets or a cooperative before you sell. If the price is high, the yield is likely good and the labor is the cost, the waiting pays off. Keep the beans in a dry place, sort out any damaged ones, and check the cooperative or ICAT to reach a larger buyer. If you need the exact price, contact a cooperative or ICAT.
